definition: To support or strengthen something, especially an argument or claim.
example: The historian buttressed her claim with letters found in the town archive.
nuance: Buttress suggests propping something up with added support, often evidence, while bolster more often means lifting spirits or confidence.
prompt: A student is preparing for a debate about later school start times.
options: She gathered sleep studies to buttress her case for starting classes at nine.
She hoped to buttress her opponent's argument by exposing every one of its weakest statistics.
She planned to buttress each of her rival's claims by proving it was false.
She kept trying to buttress into the other team's speeches with loud interruptions.
reasons: Research that backs up her position makes her argument stronger.
Exposing weak points tears an argument down instead of propping it up.
Proving a claim false means rebutting it, which is the reverse of supporting it.
This mixes the word up with "butt in"; it has nothing to do with interrupting.

practice.prompt: Workers inspect an old stone barn wall that has begun to lean outward.
options: The crew built a brick pier to buttress the barn wall against further leaning.
To buttress the wall, the crew pulled out the last wooden beams holding it upright.
The crew chose to buttress the wall by painting it a brighter shade of red.
The crew used a sharp chisel to buttress the crumbling mortar out of the gaps between stones.
reasons: A solid pier pressed against the wall gives it the extra support it needs.
Taking away supports weakens the wall rather than strengthening it.
A fresh coat of paint changes the look but adds no structural strength.
Scraping material out is removal; the word never means digging or clearing away.
